newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Germany deports non-criminal Bosnian refugees.
newsitem.headline: Germany deports non-criminal Bosnian refugees.

text.p: Germany deported 24 Bosnians on Wednesday, among them the first refugees without criminal records to be expelled since Bonn decided more than 300,000 people who fled the war would have to return.
A chartered jet flew from Munich and landed amid tight NATO security at Sarajevo airport where the 22 men and two women were handed over to the Bosnian authorities.

"We are from Bavaria. I was arrested because I drove a car without a driving licence and they put me in prison," Amar Dzanic told reporters. "I am from Banja Luka and I want to go back to Germany because I have a five-year-old child there."
Fifteen of Wednesday's deportees had been convicted of crimes but the other nine were the first group of non-criminals to be expelled.
Many of those on Wednesday's flight, including Dzanic, were Moslems from areas now in the Bosnian Serb republic where it is too dangerous for them to return.
"I've got a few addresses from my friends in Germany so I'll see where I can go," said Senad Turanovic, 35, one of those convicted, who said he left behind a wife, mother and three children.
Before being hustled to a Bosnian government police station many of the group complained to reporters they had been roused early in the morning and told they were leaving the same day.

German and Bosnia signed an agreement last month allowing the repatriation of more than 300,000 refugees from the conflict in former Yugoslavia and said they hoped many would start returning of their own free will soon.
But with much of Moslem-controlled Bosnia already crowded with displaced people that seems a forlorn hope.
Interior Minister Manfred Kanther said Germany would send back those who refused to return voluntarily, starting with the unmarried and then married couples with children.
Under the repatriation plan it is hoped 70,000 to 90,000 refugees will have left for Bosnia by mid-1997.
"We don't plan to send back large groups of refugees this year, but of course there could be some single people made to return," said Heinz Grunwald of the Bavarian interior ministry.
The repatriation plan has been opposed by some politicians and refugee groups in Germany. The Pro Asyl refugee organisation described the deportations as inhumane.
Germany welcomed more refugees from the wars of former Yugoslavia than the rest of Europe put together -- more than 400,000, 80 percent of them from Bosnia.
